newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Swift Fokker rescue hopes dented.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swift Fokker rescue hopes dented.

text.p: The chances of a swift South Korean rescue deal for Dutch planemaker Fokker took a knock on Friday when administrators of the bankrupt company said they did not expect a decision by Seoul for at least two weeks.

South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries has been given exclusive access to Fokker's books with a view to a possible takeover of its core planemaking business, but the process is taking longer than expected.
"Administrators anticipate no decision from the Korean government before the end of November," a statement from the administrators' office said.

"In the event of a positive decision, the final negotiations and conclusion of final contracts of all the parties involved would continue for some more weeks," the statement said, pushing the prospect of a final deal into the new year.
Recent Dutch media reports have suggested that a review of the rescue deal by the Seoul government might delay negotiations, but Samsung said on Wednesday it was not at issue.
"The only government approval Samsung needs is from the central bank of Korea on capital investment abroad," it said.
A South Korean government spokesman said earlier this week the government could not tell Samsung what to do about Fokker.
"It's a private project paid for by a private company," said Yu Jeong-yeol of the aerospace industry industry division at the South Korean ministry of trade.

A spokesman for the Dutch economics affairs ministry declined to add to the statement from the administrators or say if the government had a timeframe for its continued involvement in Fokker negotiations.
"The administrators are doing the negotiations with Samsung. There's a role for the Dutch government, but at the moment we cannot do anything other than wait."

Court-appointed administrators have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March following a decision by Germany's Daimler-Benz to cut off further funding of its Dutch unit. Two months ago the administrators gave Samsung exclusive rights to go through Fokker's books.
Earlier this month Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers said he expected a decision "within days" by Samsung.

Samsung Aerospace, a unit of the Samsung Group SAGR,CN, sees Fokker as a way of breaking into the global aerospace industry but is unwilling to assume all the risks of the company and wants major investment by the Netherlands.

"Samsung and the administrators of Fokker are talking about the possibility that Samsung buys Fokker and there's a role there for the Dutch government. We've seen the business plan and we came with an offer in the direction of Samsung and we're more or less waiting on an answer and so are the administrators," the economic affairs ministry spokesman said on Friday.
He declined to comment on a statement at the beginning of November by a Samsung spokesman that the Dutch government wanted a $500-$600 million long-term investment in Fokker.
The Dutch government has said it would provide capital and invest in a new 125-seat regional jet, but Samsung is said to have baulked at demands for long-term Dutch job guarantees.

Earlier this week Samsung said it had invited other domestic companies to join it in a Fokker rescue but denied this was slowing down the deal. Dutch daily newspaper De Volkskrant reported on Friday that Samsung seemed to be having no luck in interesting potential partners.
